task_description: Help me draft a follow-up email to a VP of Operations at a logistics company after our second demo — she was impressed with the routing optimization but concerned about integration with their legacy TMS.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes sales emails that feel like personal correspondence, not campaigns. Every email advances the relationship and the deal simultaneously. Treats email as a tool for creating conversations, never for closing them.

rubric.name: Specific Callback
rubric.description: Every prospect email references something specific from a prior interaction — a concern they raised, a phrase they used, a goal they mentioned. Never generic callbacks like 'as we discussed' or 'following up on our meeting.'

dimensions.label: References a specific comment, question, or concern the prospect raised in a prior interaction
The reference could not apply to a different prospect — it's unique to this person
Does not use 'as discussed', 'per our conversation', or 'following up on our meeting' without specifics

rubric.name: No Commercial Terms in Writing
rubric.description: Price, discounts, contract terms, and commercial details are never put in email. Email establishes need and books conversations. Numbers in writing before a live discussion forfeit negotiation leverage.

dimensions.label: Does not include any specific pricing, discount percentages, or contract terms
Steers toward a live meeting or call for any commercial discussion
Discusses value, outcomes, and ROI — never the cost to achieve them

rubric.name: Re-engagement Over Check-ins
rubric.description: Follow-ups after silence never 'just check in.' Each follow-up provides a new reason to respond — a relevant customer win, fresh data, a deadline, or a reframed value proposition.

dimensions.label: Each follow-up email introduces new information the prospect didn't have before
Does not use 'just checking in', 'touching base', 'wanted to follow up', or equivalent
Creates a specific, time-relevant reason for the prospect to reply

rubric.name: Risk-First Internal Updates
rubric.description: Internal deal updates lead with the risk to closing, not the opportunity. 'They're evaluating a competitor pilot' is more useful than 'great meeting, they're interested.'

dimensions.label: The first substantive sentence identifies the primary risk or blocker to the deal
The internal email requests a specific action to mitigate the risk, not just awareness
Does not lead with or overweight positive signals when risks exist

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Kofi treats every prospect email as proof he was listening — specificity is his differentiator from competitors' outreach. Non-negotiable: never put pricing in email. Will reject any follow-up that doesn't give the prospect a new reason to respond.

corrections.issue: The grader is penalizing prospect-facing emails for not meeting a criterion that only applies to internal communications. Scoring a 5 or a 1 on this criterion for a prospect email — rather than marking it not applicable and excluding it from the overall score — distorts the overall weighted score and misrepresents the email's quality. The criterion should simply not factor into the evaluation when the email type is prospect-facing.
negative_examples: Giving a prospect email a score of 5 as a 'neutral' non-applicable score, which still drags down the overall weighted average
Giving a prospect email a score of 1 because the internal update structure is 'absent', when absence is expected and correct for that email type
Treating a missing internal structure as a quality failure in a prospect email
corrections.clarification: Risk-First Internal Updates applies exclusively to internal deal communications — pipeline reviews, deal updates to management, handoff notes to other team members. When the email being evaluated is prospect-facing, this criterion should be marked not applicable and excluded entirely from scoring and weighted averages. It should never contribute a low score that penalizes an otherwise strong prospect email.

Subject: The TMS question you raised — a relevant example

Hi [Name],

After our call, I kept thinking about the integration concern you raised around your legacy TMS. That's not a small thing to work through, and I didn't want to leave it as an open question.

I wanted to share something relevant: we just completed an onboarding with a regional freight carrier that was running a 12-year-old TMS — one their team had heavily customized over the years and assumed would be the hardest part of any new implementation. Their integration was live in under three weeks, without a middleware layer, and their ops team didn't have to touch the TMS configuration to make it work.

I'm not saying your environment is identical — it may not be. But the pattern of concern is the same, and the outcome might be worth a 30-minute conversation with our implementation lead, who actually ran point on that project. He can speak to the specific connectors we used and where the edge cases showed up.

Would you be open to a call with him next week? I can have him walk through exactly how that integration was structured — no slides, just a direct technical conversation so you can pressure-test whether this is a real risk or a manageable one before you take anything further internally.

Let me know what works on your end.

Kofi

Hi [Name],

After our call, I kept thinking about the concern you raised around your legacy TMS — specifically whether an integration like this would require your team to reconfigure anything on the TMS side. That's the part I didn't want to leave unresolved.

I wanted to share something timely: we just wrapped an onboarding with a regional freight carrier running a heavily customized TMS — their words were "we've bolted so much onto this thing that nobody touches it anymore." I'd like to connect you with our implementation lead who ran that project directly. He can walk through exactly how the connectors were structured and where the edge cases surfaced — no slides, just a technical conversation so you can pressure-test whether this is a real risk or a manageable one before you take anything further internally. He has availability the week of [date], which works well given where you are in your evaluation.

Would a 30-minute call that week work for you?

Kofi

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Writes sales emails that feel like personal correspondence, not campaigns. Every email advances the relationship and the deal simultaneously. Treats email as a tool for creating conversations, never for closing them.

rubric.name: Specific Callback
rubric.description: Every prospect email references something specific from a prior interaction — a concern they raised, a phrase they used, a goal they mentioned. Never generic callbacks like 'as we discussed' or 'following up on our meeting.'

dimensions.label: References a specific comment, question, or concern the prospect raised in a prior interaction
The reference could not apply to a different prospect — it's unique to this person
Does not use 'as discussed', 'per our conversation', or 'following up on our meeting' without specifics

rubric.name: No Commercial Terms in Writing
rubric.description: Price, discounts, contract terms, and commercial details are never put in email. Email establishes need and books conversations. Numbers in writing before a live discussion forfeit negotiation leverage.

dimensions.label: Does not include any specific pricing, discount percentages, or contract terms
Steers toward a live meeting or call for any commercial discussion
Discusses value, outcomes, and ROI — never the cost to achieve them

rubric.name: Re-engagement Over Check-ins
rubric.description: Follow-ups after silence never 'just check in.' Each follow-up provides a new reason to respond — a relevant customer win, fresh data, a deadline, or a reframed value proposition.

dimensions.label: Each follow-up email introduces new information the prospect didn't have before
Does not use 'just checking in', 'touching base', 'wanted to follow up', or equivalent
Creates a specific, time-relevant reason for the prospect to reply

rubric.name: Risk-First Internal Updates
rubric.description: Internal deal updates lead with the risk to closing, not the opportunity. 'They're evaluating a competitor pilot' is more useful than 'great meeting, they're interested.'

dimensions.label: The first substantive sentence identifies the primary risk or blocker to the deal
The internal email requests a specific action to mitigate the risk, not just awareness
Does not lead with or overweight positive signals when risks exist

negative_examples: Giving a prospect email a score of 5 as a 'neutral' non-applicable score, which still drags down the overall weighted average
Giving a prospect email a score of 1 because the internal update structure is 'absent', when absence is expected and correct for that email type
Treating a missing internal structure as a quality failure in a prospect email
rubric.clarification: Risk-First Internal Updates applies exclusively to internal deal communications — pipeline reviews, deal updates to management, handoff notes to other team members. When the email being evaluated is prospect-facing, this criterion should be marked not applicable and excluded entirely from scoring and weighted averages. It should never contribute a low score that penalizes an otherwise strong prospect email.

rubric_snapshot.coaching_notes: Kofi treats every prospect email as proof he was listening — specificity is his differentiator from competitors' outreach. Non-negotiable: never put pricing in email. Will reject any follow-up that doesn't give the prospect a new reason to respond.
